title: Attend to your own soul
hook: no one is unhappy for ignoring another's mind, only their own (Meditations 2.8)

segments.voice: Yesterday: stop being whirled around, by outside things or by aimless busyness. Your line was stop spinning. What did you stop, and what did you learn instead? Day five hundred thirty-four.

She replied with just okay. Not okay with an exclamation point. Not sounds good. Just okay, with a period. What did she mean? Is she annoyed? Was it something I said on Tuesday? Twenty minutes later you're still turning it over, and you've screenshotted it to a friend for a second opinion. We spend a startling amount of the day trying to read other people's minds. In book two, Marcus makes a blunt observation about where that attention would be better spent. Today: attend to your own soul.
screen: `OKAY. WITH A PERIOD.` → `READING OTHER PEOPLE'S MINDS.` → `ATTEND TO YOUR OWN SOUL.`

segments.voice: First, the line. Section eight is two sentences. Hardly anyone, Marcus says, has been seen to be unhappy because they didn't notice what was going on in someone else's mind. But people who don't follow the movements of their own minds are bound to be unhappy. Second, the honest word. He doesn't say never. He says hardly anyone, or seldom. Of course there are times when misreading someone costs us. Marcus isn't pretending otherwise. He's pointing at where most of the unhappiness comes from. Third, the movements of the mind. For the Stoics, the mind is always moving. An impression arrives: she's annoyed with me. Then comes a moment when you agree to it, or don't. Then an impulse: send a worried text, go cold, rehearse an argument. Watching those movements, catching the impression before you agree to it, is the whole practice. Epictetus said it in his handbook, which opened this year: test the impression first. Marcus is writing the same lesson to himself. Fourth, where to point the flashlight. You can't see into her mind, however long you stare at the word okay. You can see into your own. You can notice the story you're telling, the fear under it, the reaction you're about to have. That's the one mind you can actually tend. This isn't selfishness. Elsewhere in this same book, Marcus says we were made to work together, like hands or feet. Attending to your own soul is what makes you safe to be around. It's how the okay with a period stops running your afternoon.
screen: `NOT KNOWING THEIR MIND: SELDOM MISERY.` · `NOT WATCHING YOUR OWN: ALWAYS.` · `IMPRESSION, AGREEMENT, IMPULSE.` · `POINT THE FLASHLIGHT INWARD.` · then, large: `MIND MY OWN MIND.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Check in with yourself, the way Marcus suggests. What's moving in your mind right now? A worry, a plan, a replay of a conversation? Name it, quietly. Then ask: is this about my own mind, or am I guessing at someone else's? If you're guessing, gently bring the flashlight back. What are you feeling, under the guess? Stay there. The bell holds the time.
Attend to your own soul. Few are made unhappy by not reading another's mind; those who don't watch their own are bound to be. Today's word.
screen: `ATTEND TO YOUR OWN SOUL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: mind my own mind. Three times today, stop and ask what's moving in your own mind, especially when you catch yourself guessing at someone else's. Day five hundred thirty-four.

howItsDone: Many people practicing Stoicism do brief check-ins during the day, noticing their own impressions and reactions instead of trying to decode what others are thinking.

original.note: Greek: soul, life, mind. Marcus watches the 'movements' of his own.

trapdoor: what you thought: mind your own business.
what it means: watch the movements of your own mind; that's where most unhappiness starts, and the one place you can tend.
what a scholar hears: 'movements' of the soul echo Stoic theory of impression, assent and impulse, the core of Epictetus' teaching.

notes: Meditations 2.8 paraphrased (Long: 'Through not observing what is in the mind of another a man has seldom been observed to be unhappy; but those who do not observe the movements of their own minds must of necessity be unhappy.'). Confirm.
Greek ψυχή in 2.8 ('the movements of one's own soul'): confirm.
'Test the impression first' ties to Enchiridion 1.5 ('you are an impression, and not at all the thing you appear to be'), taught in Block A. Confirm reference.
